title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction: Problem: decide whether a large N is prime by testing whether it has a second representation by a binary quadratic form. §1: First write N = a² + λb², then look for another representation N = x² + λy². If one exists, N is composite and a factor can be computed. From a² − x² = λ(y² − b²) we get (a+x)/(y+b) = λ(y−b)/(a−x). Write this common ratio in lowest terms as λ·p/q and put a+x = λmp, y−b = np, y+b = mq, a−x = nq. Then a = (λmp+nq)/2, x = (λmp−nq)/2, b = (mq−np)/2, y = (mq+np)/2. Substituting gives N = ¼(λm²+n²)(λp²+q²). So λp²+q², or its half, or its quarter, divides N. This is the composition identity for x²+λy² run backwards, and it is how Euler turns two representations into a factor. §2 begins the search procedure. Parity and residues mod 8 fix whether x or y is even. One then sets N − λy² = x² (with x chosen so that λ | N − x²) or N − x² = λy². Splitting the unknown into even and odd cases gives new quadratic conditions 'quadratum fieri debet', which are worked out on the next pages for N = 10003 = 100² + 3·1² = 16² + 3·57², giving the factor 7. The left-hand page is the end of the preceding piece (E718). It tabulates the a ≤ 299 for which 232a² + 1 is prime; 232 is one of Euler's idoneal numbers, and 232·299² ≈ 20.7 million, matching 'ad 20 milliones'.
errors: The rule in §1 that λp²+q², its half, or its quarter divides N is incomplete. The substitution a+x = λmp, y+b = mq presumes λ is coprime to q, which need not hold. In Euler's own example (§8, next page), (a+x)/(y+b) = 116/58 = 2 = 3·(2/3), so q = 3 shares the factor λ = 3. Then m = 58/3 is not an integer, and λp²+q² = 21 does not divide 10003 at all (only 7 does). Euler silently repairs this by dividing by 3 ('per 3 depressum'). The general statement should allow removing a divisor of λ (more generally, take gcds), not only factors 2 and 4.

Minor: §1 does not say that the second representation must be essentially different (x ≠ ±a). It also does not say that the resulting factor could be trivial in degenerate cases, for example when N has square factors or common factors with λ.

ideas.what: Two distinct representations of N by x²+λy² imply N is composite, with an explicit factor via a² − x² = λ(y² − b²) and reduction of the ratio to lowest terms
ideas.modern_name: Euler's factorization method (generalized to forms x²+ny²); uniqueness of representation of primes by a form
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (λ = 1 case in 1745–1749 correspondence with Goldbach and in his sums-of-two-squares papers; general λ in his late idoneal-number papers)
ideas.where_published: Euler's late papers on numeri idonei and primality testing (E708, E715, E718, E719, E725 and neighbours); discussed in Dickson's History vol. I and Weil's Number Theory
Euler's Algebra and many number-theory papers

ideas.what: Narrowing the search for a second representation using parity and residues mod 8, then splitting into cases
ideas.modern_name: sieve by congruence conditions (exclusion method, as in Gauss DA §§319ff)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; later systematized by Gauss (method of exclusion)
ideas.where_published: E708, E719 and related papers; Gauss Disquisitiones §§319–322

deep.surprise_reason: The page states Euler's well-known factoring-by-two-representations principle for x²+λy². This is documented in Dickson and Weil and in Euler's cluster of idoneal-number papers. The only notable point is a small gap: the 'half or quarter' rule fails when λ shares a factor with q, which Euler's own example exhibits and he patches ad hoc.
transcription_corrections: Left page formula '3?aa+1' is '232aa+1' (232 is an idoneal number; 232·299² + 1 ≈ 20.7 million, matching 'ad 20 milliones').
'fractiones ad minimos terminos reducti sint' should read 'reductae'; in the print, '÷' and '=' are confused in several places (e.g. 'N = aa + λbb').
Left page: list ends at 299 and the heading lines read '28| 282, 284, 286, 287' and '29| 290, 292, 293, 295, 296, 298'.
